title: Thread vs Runnable: Creating and Starting Threads
description: Create threads by extending Thread and by implementing Runnable. Understand why Runnable is preferred, and use Thread.start(), join(), and sleep().
hints: Extend Thread and override run(); or implement Runnable and pass it to new Thread(runnable).
Always call start() — NEVER call run() directly (run() executes on the current thread).
join() blocks the calling thread until the target thread terminates.
Thread.currentThread().getName() returns the thread's name.

solution.explanation: Extending Thread couples your task logic to the threading mechanism. Implementing Runnable (or using a lambda) separates the what (the task) from the how (the thread), and it's more flexible — the same Runnable can be submitted to an ExecutorService later. NEVER call run() directly: it executes synchronously on the calling thread, not on a new thread. start() allocates a new OS thread and calls run() asynchronously. join() is the key to synchronisation: main() calls t1.join() and blocks until t1's run() returns. sleep() suspends the current thread for at least the given number of milliseconds — it's interruptible, so always catch InterruptedException and re-set the interrupt flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt().

methodSignatures.description: Starts a new OS thread and calls run() on it asynchronously.
Blocks the calling thread until this thread terminates.
Static. Suspends the current thread for at least millis milliseconds.
Static. Returns the Thread object for the currently executing thread.

title: Daemon Threads and Thread Interrupt
description: Understand daemon threads (background threads that don't prevent JVM shutdown), and learn the proper interrupt-and-check pattern for stoppable threads.
hints: Call thread.setDaemon(true) BEFORE thread.start() — can't change after starting.
For interruptible loops: while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) { ... }
When sleep() is interrupted, it clears the interrupt flag and throws InterruptedException — re-set the flag.
The JVM exits when all non-daemon threads have finished — daemon threads are killed without cleanup.

solution.explanation: Daemon threads are JVM-managed background threads: the JVM does NOT wait for them to finish before exiting. Common use cases: garbage collection (the GC threads are daemons), heartbeat monitors, log flushers. Non-daemon (user) threads are what keep the JVM alive. Thread interruption is a cooperative mechanism — you can't forcibly stop a thread. interrupt() sets a flag on the thread. The thread must periodically check isInterrupted() (or call a blocking method like sleep/wait/join that throws InterruptedException when interrupted). The crucial pattern after catching InterruptedException: immediately re-call Thread.currentThread().interrupt() to restore the flag, because sleep() clears it when throwing. Then exit cleanly. Never swallow InterruptedException silently.

methodSignatures.description: Marks this thread as daemon or non-daemon; must be called before start().
Sets the interrupt flag on the target thread.
Tests whether this thread's interrupt flag is set (does not clear the flag).
Static. Tests and CLEARS the current thread's interrupt flag.

title: Race Condition and synchronized: Fixing Shared Counter
description: Observe a race condition on a shared counter incremented by multiple threads, then fix it with synchronized methods and synchronized blocks.
hints: counter++ is actually three steps: read, add 1, write. Threads can interleave these steps.
'synchronized' on an instance method locks on 'this' — only one thread can hold it at a time.
A synchronized block: synchronized(lockObject) { ... } gives you finer control over the scope.
Reset counter to 0 between runs of the test.

solution.explanation: counter++ compiles to three bytecodes: GETFIELD (read), IADD (increment), PUTFIELD (write). If Thread A reads counter=5 and Thread B also reads counter=5 before A writes back 6, both write 6, and one increment is lost — this is a race condition. synchronized on an instance method acquires the intrinsic (monitor) lock on 'this'. Only one thread can hold this lock at a time; others block at the method entry. synchronized blocks let you narrow the critical section — useful when the method does expensive non-synchronized setup before the actual shared-state modification. Both approaches guarantee mutual exclusion AND visibility: the happens-before relationship in the JMM guarantees that all writes made while holding the lock are visible to any thread that subsequently acquires it.

methodSignatures.description: Acquires the intrinsic lock on 'this' for the duration of the method.
Acquires the intrinsic lock on 'obj' for the duration of the block.

title: Volatile and Double-Checked Locking
description: Implement a lazy-initialised singleton with correct double-checked locking using volatile. Understand why volatile is required and what broken DCL looks like.
hints: Without volatile, the JIT/CPU can reorder: the pointer to the new object can be published BEFORE the constructor finishes.
volatile prevents instruction reordering: write to instance is visible and ordered w.r.t. the constructor.
The holder pattern uses class loading as a synchronisation mechanism — classes are loaded lazily and exactly once.

solution.explanation: The Java Memory Model allows the JIT compiler and CPU to reorder instructions for performance, provided they appear equivalent in a single-threaded context. new Singleton() compiles to: (1) allocate memory, (2) call constructor, (3) assign to instance. The JIT can reorder steps 2 and 3 — this is safe for a single thread but catastrophic for DCL: Thread B can see instance != null and read a partially constructed object. volatile prohibits this: a write to a volatile variable establishes a happens-before relationship with all subsequent reads of that variable, preventing reordering across the volatile write. The Holder pattern avoids all of this: inner static classes are loaded lazily (only when first referenced) and class initialisation is guaranteed to be atomic by the JVM class loading protocol. This is the cleanest lazy singleton in Java. For simplicity without lazy init, use enum singleton (see design-patterns exercises).

methodSignatures.description: Keyword. Guarantees visibility and ordering for all reads/writes; prevents caching in registers.

title: ReentrantLock: lock/unlock, tryLock, and Fairness
description: Use ReentrantLock as an explicit alternative to synchronized. Demonstrate lock/unlock in a try-finally block, tryLock() for non-blocking acquisition, and fair vs unfair mode.
hints: Always release in finally: lock.lock(); try { ... } finally { lock.unlock(); }
tryLock() returns immediately (true if acquired, false if not); tryLock(time, unit) waits up to the timeout.
new ReentrantLock(true) creates a FAIR lock — threads acquire in FIFO order (slower but no starvation).
A reentrant lock: the thread that holds the lock can call lock() again without deadlocking.

solution.explanation: ReentrantLock offers capabilities that synchronized cannot: timed tryLock (avoids deadlock by giving up after a timeout), interruptible lock acquisition (lockInterruptibly()), fair mode, and Condition variables (a replacement for wait/notify). The try-finally pattern around lock/unlock is non-negotiable — if the critical section throws an exception and unlock() is not in finally, the lock is never released and all other threads will deadlock. Reentrant means the thread that already holds the lock can acquire it again — this is required for recursive methods that call other synchronized methods. Each successful lock() must have a matching unlock(), so getHoldCount() being 2 means unlock() must be called twice. Fair mode (new ReentrantLock(true)) queues threads in arrival order; unfair mode allows barging, which has higher throughput but can starve waiting threads.

title: ReentrantReadWriteLock: Concurrent Reads, Exclusive Writes
description: Use ReentrantReadWriteLock to allow multiple threads to read simultaneously while writes are exclusive. Model a cached value with read-dominated access.
hints: rwLock.readLock().lock() allows concurrent reads; rwLock.writeLock().lock() is exclusive.
A write lock can only be acquired when no read or write lock is held by any thread.
Prefer ReadWriteLock when: reads are much more frequent than writes, and reads take non-trivial time.

solution.explanation: A ReadWriteLock maintains a pair of associated locks: a read lock that can be held simultaneously by multiple reader threads (as long as there's no writer), and a write lock that is exclusive. This dramatically improves throughput when reads dominate, compared to using synchronized or a plain ReentrantLock which would serialise all access. The invariants: (1) any number of readers can hold the read lock concurrently, (2) only one writer can hold the write lock, (3) a writer blocks until all readers release, and readers block while a writer holds the lock. In Java, the ReentrantReadWriteLock does NOT support upgrading a read lock to a write lock — you must release the read lock first, risking that another writer slips in. For that use case, consider StampedLock (Java 8) which supports optimistic reads.

methodSignatures.description: Returns the shared read lock; multiple threads can acquire it simultaneously.
Returns the exclusive write lock; blocks all other readers and writers.

title: ExecutorService: submit Callable, Future.get, invokeAll
description: Use Executors.newFixedThreadPool() to manage a pool of threads. Submit Callable tasks to get Future results, invoke multiple tasks at once with invokeAll, and shut down cleanly.
hints: Callable<T> is like Runnable but returns T and can throw checked exceptions.
Future<T>.get() blocks until the result is ready; get(timeout, unit) times out if too slow.
invokeAll(Collection<Callable<T>>) returns List<Future<T>> in the same order as input.
Always call shutdown() after submitting all tasks; then awaitTermination() to wait for them.

solution.explanation: ExecutorService decouples task submission from thread lifecycle management. A fixed thread pool reuses a set of threads, avoiding the overhead of creating/destroying threads per task. Callable is the parametrised, exception-aware version of Runnable — the return value is wrapped in a Future. Future.get() is a blocking call — it waits until the task completes and returns the result, or throws ExecutionException if the task threw an exception (wrap/unwrap the cause). invokeAll() submits all tasks and blocks until every Future is done — useful when you need ALL results. invokeAny() submits all and returns the first successful result, cancelling the others — useful for redundant requests where only one answer is needed. Shutdown sequence: shutdown() prevents new submissions, awaitTermination() waits gracefully, shutdownNow() interrupts running tasks.

methodSignatures.description: Submits a Callable for execution and returns a Future.
Blocks until the task completes and returns the result.
Submits all tasks and blocks until all complete.
Returns the result of the first successful task; cancels the rest.
Blocks until all tasks finish or timeout expires after shutdown().

title: AtomicInteger and AtomicReference: Lock-Free Operations
description: Use AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() and compareAndSet() for lock-free thread-safe operations. Understand why volatile alone is not sufficient for compound operations like i++.
hints: volatile ensures visibility but NOT atomicity. i++ is still read-modify-write under volatile.
compareAndSet(expected, update): atomically sets to update if current == expected; else returns false.
AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() is a single atomic machine instruction (LOCK XADD on x86).
For AtomicReference, use a loop: while (!ref.compareAndSet(oldVal, newVal)) — spin until CAS succeeds.

solution.explanation: volatile guarantees that reads/writes go directly to main memory and are never cached in a CPU register or L1 cache — it ensures visibility. But it does NOT make compound operations like i++ atomic. i++ is still read-modify-write, and two threads can interleave at the read step, both reading the same old value and both writing the same new value, losing one increment. AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() maps to a single hardware instruction (on x86: LOCK XADD) that atomically reads, increments, and writes in one indivisible step. compareAndSet(expected, update) is the fundamental CAS (Compare-And-Swap) instruction: it atomically checks if the current value equals expected, and if so, replaces it with update. The CAS loop retries if it loses a race — this is called optimistic concurrency. It avoids lock overhead and is never subject to deadlock, but can spin under very high contention.

methodSignatures.description: Atomically increments and returns the new value.
Atomically sets to update if current == expect; returns true on success.
Atomically sets reference to update if current == expect.

title: ConcurrentHashMap vs Synchronized HashMap
description: Understand why ConcurrentHashMap outperforms Collections.synchronizedMap() in concurrent environments, and use compute(), merge(), and putIfAbsent() for atomic compound operations.
hints: ConcurrentHashMap uses segment-level locking (Java 7) or CAS+striped locks (Java 8) — no global lock.
computeIfAbsent / compute / merge are atomic — use them instead of get() + put() pairs.
merge(key, 1, Integer::sum) is the cleanest way to count word frequencies.
Collections.synchronizedMap() wraps every method in 'synchronized(this)' — a global lock, terrible throughput.

solution.explanation: Collections.synchronizedMap() wraps the underlying map with a mutex on every method — reads and writes are serialised through a single lock. ConcurrentHashMap in Java 8 uses a much finer-grained approach: reads are lock-free (using volatile), writes lock only the affected bucket using CAS, and resize uses a concurrent transfer protocol. This gives near-linear scaling with thread count for read-heavy workloads. The critical insight: even with ConcurrentHashMap, the sequence get() then put() is NOT atomic — there's a race window between the two calls. Use the atomic compound operations: computeIfAbsent() (run the function and store the result if key is absent), compute() (always run the function with old value), and merge() (merge a value with an existing one using a BiFunction). merge(key, 1, Integer::sum) is the idiomatic word-counter pattern: if key is absent, put 1; if present, add 1 to the existing count.

title: BlockingQueue: Producer-Consumer with LinkedBlockingQueue
description: Implement the classic producer-consumer pattern using LinkedBlockingQueue. Use put() (blocks when full) and take() (blocks when empty) to coordinate work between threads.
hints: LinkedBlockingQueue(capacity) creates a bounded queue — put() blocks when capacity is reached.
take() blocks the consumer thread until an item is available — no busy-waiting.
The poison-pill pattern: producer sends a special sentinel value; consumer exits when it receives it.
For multiple consumers, send one poison pill per consumer.

solution.explanation: BlockingQueue is the cleanest way to implement producer-consumer in Java. put() blocks the producer when the queue is full — this provides automatic back-pressure, preventing the producer from overwhelming the consumer. take() blocks the consumer when the queue is empty — no busy-waiting, which would waste CPU. The consumer is slower (300ms) than the producer (100ms), so the queue fills up and put() blocks the producer — you'll see batches of tasks queued before each consumer read. The poison-pill pattern is the cleanest shutdown mechanism for bounded queues: the producer sends a sentinel value that signals the consumer to stop. For N consumers, send N poison pills. Alternative: use an AtomicBoolean 'running' flag and poll(timeout) instead of take() — useful when you need the consumer to be interruptible. ArrayBlockingQueue pre-allocates the array (predictable memory), LinkedBlockingQueue uses linked nodes (lower contention between head and tail operations).

methodSignatures.description: Inserts element, blocking until space is available.
Retrieves and removes head element, blocking until one is available.
Retrieves head, waiting up to timeout; returns null on timeout.

title: CountDownLatch: Wait for Multiple Events
description: Use CountDownLatch to make threads wait for a set of one-time events. Model a race starting gate and a results aggregation scenario.
hints: new CountDownLatch(N) — count starts at N; latch.await() blocks until count reaches 0.
latch.countDown() decrements by 1; cannot be reset — CountDownLatch is single-use.
For a starting gate: count=1; all runners call await() before their work; starter calls countDown().
For completion tracking: count=N (number of workers); each worker calls countDown() when done.

solution.explanation: CountDownLatch is a one-shot synchroniser: it starts at count N and decrements to 0; any thread calling await() blocks until it reaches 0. Once at 0, all waiting threads are released and it cannot be reset. Two classical patterns: (1) Starting gate — count=1, N threads call await(), then one thread calls countDown() to fire all at once, useful for benchmarks that need N threads to start simultaneously. (2) Completion latch — count=N, main waits, each worker calls countDown() when done, main resumes when all complete. Unlike join(), a CountDownLatch doesn't require a reference to each thread. Also, it allows a thread to countDown multiple times (though usually once per worker) and supports timeouts via await(time, unit). For a repeatable barrier (where threads should wait multiple rounds), use CyclicBarrier instead.

methodSignatures.description: Creates a latch initialised to count.

title: CyclicBarrier and Semaphore
description: Use CyclicBarrier to make a group of threads meet at a point repeatedly (e.g. parallel computation phases). Use Semaphore to limit concurrent access to a resource (e.g. connection pool).
hints: new CyclicBarrier(N, barrierAction) — N threads must call await() before any can proceed.
CyclicBarrier resets automatically after each cycle — can be reused for multi-phase computation.
new Semaphore(permits) — acquire() blocks if no permits available; release() returns a permit.
Semaphore.acquire() / release() are analogous to a ticket: you must hold a ticket to enter.

solution.explanation: CyclicBarrier is the multi-party, reusable counterpart to CountDownLatch. All N parties must call await() before any can proceed — think of it as a meeting point. After all arrive, the optional barrier action runs (on the last-arriving thread), then all threads are released. The 'cyclic' part: the barrier resets automatically, so the same CyclicBarrier can be used for phase 2, phase 3, etc. BrokenBarrierException is thrown to all waiting threads if one is interrupted or times out — the barrier is then in a broken state. Semaphore models N available permits. acquire() decrements permits (blocks at 0); release() increments. This naturally implements a bounded resource pool. Unlike a mutex (which is fair to exactly 1 thread), Semaphore(1) is a binary semaphore (mutex), Semaphore(N) allows N concurrent holders. Fair mode (true) queues waiters in FIFO order, preventing starvation.

methodSignatures.description: Blocks until all parties have called await(); returns arrival index.

Returns the current number of available permits.

title: CopyOnWriteArrayList: Safe Iteration Without Locking
description: Use CopyOnWriteArrayList when you have infrequent writes and many concurrent reads/iterations. Understand why it's safe to iterate without a lock and when NOT to use it.
hints: ArrayList fails fast: it uses a modCount to detect structural modification during iteration.
CopyOnWriteArrayList: every write creates a NEW backing array — iterators work on the old snapshot.
Use CopyOnWriteArrayList for listener/observer lists where writes are rare but reads (notifications) are frequent.
Never use CopyOnWriteArrayList for high-write workloads — O(n) copy per write is prohibitive.

solution.explanation: ArrayList is not thread-safe: it tracks modifications with an internal modCount. Its iterator checks modCount at each step and throws ConcurrentModificationException if it has changed. CopyOnWriteArrayList solves this by making writes create a completely new copy of the backing array — iterators always work on an immutable snapshot from when they were created. This means readers never block (no locks), and adding/removing elements while iterating is safe. The trade-off: every add/remove/set is O(n) because it copies the entire array. This is fine for small observer/listener lists that are registered at startup and rarely change, but catastrophic for a list with millions of items and frequent writes. Also note: iterator snapshots see a view of the list as it was at iterator creation — elements added after are not visible to an existing iterator.

methodSignatures.description: Creates a copy-on-write list pre-populated with c.

title: ThreadLocal: Per-Thread State Without Synchronization
description: Use ThreadLocal to give each thread its own isolated copy of a value — eliminating sharing and the need for synchronization. Classic use cases: SimpleDateFormat, database connections, user sessions.
hints: ThreadLocal.withInitial(Supplier<T>) creates a ThreadLocal with a lazy initialiser — called once per thread.
threadLocal.get() returns the value for the current thread; threadLocal.set(val) sets it.
IMPORTANT: Always call remove() in finally when using ThreadLocal with thread pools — or you'll get stale data leaking across tasks.
Each thread gets its own isolated copy — no synchronisation needed.

solution.explanation: ThreadLocal<T> provides each thread with its own isolated variable — conceptually like a Map<Thread, T> where the key is always Thread.currentThread(). There's no sharing, so there's no synchronisation needed. SimpleDateFormat is the classic use case: it's expensive to create and not thread-safe, so creating one per request is wasteful, and one shared instance causes data corruption. ThreadLocal.withInitial(Supplier) lazily creates the value on the first call to get() per thread — perfect for this pattern. The critical warning about thread pools: ExecutorService reuses threads across tasks. If a task sets a ThreadLocal value without removing it in finally, the next task on that thread inherits the stale value — a notoriously hard-to-diagnose bug. Always call remove() in a finally block when using ThreadLocal with pooled threads. This is why frameworks like Spring manage their own ThreadLocal cleanup.

methodSignatures.description: Creates a ThreadLocal whose initial value is computed by the supplier on first access per thread.
Returns the current thread's value; initialises if first call.
Sets the current thread's value.
Removes the current thread's value — critical in thread pools to prevent leaks.

title: CompletableFuture: Async Pipelines and Exception Handling
description: Build non-blocking async pipelines with CompletableFuture. Chain computations with thenApply/thenCompose, combine futures with thenCombine, and handle errors with exceptionally.
hints: supplyAsync(Supplier) runs on the ForkJoinPool.commonPool() by default; pass an Executor as 2nd arg to use your own pool.
thenApply(Function) transforms the result synchronously; thenCompose(Function) chains with another async step.
thenCombine(other, BiFunction) waits for two futures to complete and merges their results.
exceptionally(Function<Throwable,T>) provides a fallback value on exception — like a catch block.

solution.explanation: CompletableFuture is Java's answer to asynchronous, non-blocking pipelines. supplyAsync() submits work to a thread pool and immediately returns a Future — the calling thread doesn't block. thenApply(fn) transforms the result when it arrives (synchronous step); thenCompose(fn) chains another async step, avoiding nested futures (like flatMap in streams). thenCombine(other, fn) runs TWO futures in parallel and calls fn with both results when both complete — total time is max(f1, f2) not sum. exceptionally(fn) is the catch block of async code: if any prior stage threw an exception, fn is called with the Throwable and provides a recovery value. CompletableFuture.allOf() creates a future that completes when ALL input futures complete — use it to synchronise parallel work. join() is like get() but throws unchecked exceptions — preferred inside lambda chains.

methodSignatures.description: Runs supplier asynchronously in the common pool; returns a future.
Chains an async step; flattens nested futures.
Combines two futures when both complete.
